AbstractText.Label: INTRODUCTION
AbstractText.content: In older patients, psychiatric illnesses frequently exist in tandem with physical illnesses, requiring nursing care that is specific to these combined care needs. The impact of caring for these patients on the mental well-being of nursing staff is unknown.

AbstractText.Label: AIM
AbstractText.content: To investigate if care characteristics of patients with combined care needs are related to the mental well-being of nursing staff.

AbstractText.Label: METHOD
AbstractText.content: Well-being of nursing staff was studied within a larger exploratory observational cross-sectional study that examined the differences and similarities of specialised combined care units in Dutch mental health care and nursing home settings.

AbstractText.Label: RESULTS
AbstractText.content: Nursing staff across settings, with more than 5 years' of work experience, felt competent in caring for patients with combined care needs. No significant effects of care characteristics of patients with combined care needs on the work-related well-being of nursing staff were shown. Both mental health nursing staff and older employees, however, were found to be more at risk of burnout.

AbstractText.Label: IMPLICATIONS/CONCLUSION
AbstractText.content: Staff well-being might benefit from placing patients with combined care needs together, so care is focused. The presence of specialised care units can allow for both targeted and focused allocation of nursing staff to these units and provision of specific training. This article is protected by copyright.
